name: The largest island as land is reclaimed
brief:
A port authority reclaims land from a bay mapped as a grid of `rows` by `cols` water cells. `fills` lists the cells `[r, c]` turned into land, in order; a cell may be listed again, which changes nothing. An island is a group of land cells joined through shared sides. After each fill, record the area of the largest island, in cells. Return the list of records.

Write `largest_after_each(rows, cols, fills)`.

Example. On a 2 by 3 bay, the fills `[[0, 0], [1, 2], [0, 1], [0, 2]]` give `[1, 1, 2, 4]`. The fourth fill joins the pair on the top row to the cell below it.
constraints: $1 \le$ `rows`, `cols` $\le 1{,}000$, and at most $100{,}000$ fills, each a cell of the grid.
Near $O(k)$ time is the target for $k$ fills. Measuring the island again after each fill is too slow once one island grows large.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Keep a union-find over the land cells with the size of each group at its root. A new cell starts as a group of one and joins each land neighbour's group, once per distinct root. The largest group never shrinks, so keep a running best.

examples.note: The last fill joins the top pair to the cell below it, an island of 4.
Filling cell `[0, 1]` again changes nothing; cell `[0, 2]` then joins all three.

tests.call: (lambda r: (len(r), r[-1], r[49999], sum(r) % 1000003))(largest_after_each(250, 400, [[i, j if i % 2 == 0 else 399 - j] for i in range(250) for j in range(400)]))

how: Submit runs 14 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value. The obvious method measures the new cell's island again with a flood fill after every fill. Once one island holds most of the cells that is a long walk per fill, and it runs out of time on the large tests. The step to the target is union-find with the group sizes kept at the roots, so each fill costs a few root lookups. Unlike counting islands as land is added, the record is the largest island's area, so each group carries its size.
notes: Islands only ever merge, so union-find with sizes at the roots tracks every island as the fills arrive.
Two neighbours of a new cell may already share an island, so a merge happens only between different roots, and a repeated fill is skipped.
With union by size and shortened climbs each fill costs close to $O(1)$, so the work is near $O(k)$.

planted.slip: Starting a repeated fill as a new group counts that cell a second time when it rejoins its island.
Recording the new cell's island, not the largest so far, drops the record when a fill starts a small island.
Measuring the new cell's island again after each fill is right but walks the whole island each time, too slow once it grows large.
